outcome: The general Zariski multiplicity conjecture (homeomorphic hypersurface germs have equal multiplicity) remains open, but a central and long-studied case — the 'multiplicity conjecture in families' (a family of isolated hypersurface singularities with constant Milnor number has constant multiplicity) — was proved by Fernández de Bobadilla and Pełka; the proof was finalized and published in the window (final arXiv revision v5, 5 March 2024; journal publication in Annals of Mathematics, online 3 July 2024). Two further special cases (a metric/bi-Lipschitz version for multiplicity two, and the 1-parameter quasihomogeneous surface-germ case) were proved in preprints posted September 2025.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet states the general 1971 Zariski multiplicity conjecture: that topological (homeomorphism) equisingularity of two reduced complex hypersurface germs implies equal algebraic multiplicity. That general statement is still open — no counterexample and no general proof exists. However, the most heavily studied restricted case, the 'multiplicity conjecture in families' (a 1-parameter family of isolated hypersurface singularities with constant Milnor number has constant multiplicity), was resolved by Javier Fernández de Bobadilla and Tomasz Pełka in 'Symplectic monodromy at radius zero and equimultiplicity of μ-constant families.' The arXiv preprint (2204.07007) was first posted 14 April 2022, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen-revision date, so the mathematical argument itself predates the window. But the paper underwent substantial revision through review: the final, accepted version (v5) was posted 5 March 2024, and the peer-reviewed article appeared in the Annals of Mathematics (Vol. 200, Issue 1), published online 3 July 2024 — both inside the window. Following §6.3's rule to date by the first written argument, and given that the argument continued to be revised until the version accepted for publication, I date the event to the final arXiv revision (5 March 2024), noting the July 2024 Annals publication as confirming expert digestion (this is what makes the classification 'partial'/resolved-in-scope rather than merely 'claimed'). The BCAM and Ikerbasque press releases (undated but clearly post-publication, referring to it as solving a '54-year-old conjecture') publicized the result but added nothing new to the underlying proof or AI question. Because the family case is a restriction of the general conjecture's scope (constant Milnor number is a special hypothesis, not present in the general statement), this counts as a 'case settled' under §3.1, hence status 'partial' rather than 'resolved' for the bullet as stated — the general conjecture is not closed. Two further, narrower special cases were resolved in September 2025 preprints (not yet digested by outside experts as of this research): Fernandes, Jelonek and Sampaio (arXiv:2509.03447, submitted 3 September 2025) proved a metric/bi-Lipschitz version of the conjecture for hypersurfaces of multiplicity exactly two (this paper does not use the name 'Zariski multiplicity conjecture' itself but proves the analogous bi-Lipschitz statement for multiplicity-two germs, framed as part of the Arnold corank problem); da Silva and Messias da Silva Júnior (arXiv:2509.01634, submitted 1 September 2025) proved Zariski's multiplicity conjecture for 1-parameter families of quasihomogeneous, corank-1, finitely-determined surface germs, a case not covered by the 2024 Annals paper (which is limited to isolated hypersurface singularities in the μ-constant-family setting; the quasihomogeneous surface germ case involves non-isolated map germs from (ℂ²,0) to (ℂ³,0)). None of the sources examined — the two 2024/2022 arXiv versions, the Annals publication page, the BCAM and Ikerbasque press releases, the two September 2025 preprints, or the related August 2023 TQFT re-proof of the family case (arXiv:2308.13925, using Floer cohomology) — mention any AI system, machine learning tool, or computer-assisted search. All proofs are traditional human mathematical arguments (symplectic geometry, Floer-theoretic/TQFT methods, weighted-degree/transverse-slice arguments). AI role is therefore 'none'.
competing_reading: One could argue the entire event should be classified 'open_stale' on the theory that the substantive mathematical content was already complete and essentially public via the April 2022 arXiv v1 preprint, making the 'event' predate the frozen revision and the later revisions/publication merely bureaucratic. Under that reading the correct status would be 'open_stale' rather than 'partial', since nothing new was mathematically discovered after January 2024, only certified/published. I did not adopt this reading because the paper continued to undergo genuine revision (five versions over nearly two years, with the final v5 explicit dated after the frozen revision, and full independent expert vetting only completing with Annals acceptance and July 2024 publication) — per §6.3's guidance to date by 'the first written argument' balanced against §6.1's definition of open_stale as work 'settled before the frozen revision's date,' the fact that the community only received a peer-reviewed, fully checked version in mid-2024 supports treating the confirmed/digested result as occurring in the window. A stricter reader could reasonably classify this as open_stale instead.
what_would_settle_it: Comparing the mathematical content of arXiv v1 (April 2022) against the final published version (July 2024 Annals) to see whether the proof strategy or key lemmas changed materially during review, which would confirm whether the 'event' genuinely happened in the window or was already complete beforehand.
